The school tree

Tuesday, 18 October 2033. The school on rue Dumenge has signed up for the “A tree for every school” programme. Mrs Chevalier, Rose-Hélène’s teacher, is preparing the planting with Dr Lefèvre, the city botanist.
Thank you for coming, doctor. The children have voted: it will be a silver lime.
Excellent choice. Its leaves have a white underside that reflects the sun, so that it suffers less from the heat.
When will we be able to plant it?
Mid-November. The soil needs to be damp so that the roots can settle before the cold.
And where should we put it? The playground is small.
Near the wall, on the south side. But not too close, in case the roots damage the foundations.
Last summer it was so hot that all the shrubs in the playground died.
I know. The soil was so dry you’d have thought it was sand. Hence the importance of watering regularly in the first year.
The children can take care of it. To give them responsibility, I was thinking of making a watering calendar.
Very good idea. And during the holidays?
The caretaker has promised to come by, so the tree will never be left alone.
Perfect. I’ll come on 15 November with a stake, for the planting. Prepare the children: it will be their tree for twenty years.

1. Consequence: si bien que, de sorte que, au point que, d’où
Consequence connectors are followed by the INDICATIVE (the consequence is a real fact):
neutral consequence
Le gardien passera, si bien que l’arbre ne sera jamais seul.
de sorte que
consequence (formal)
Les feuilles renvoient le soleil, de sorte qu’il souffre moins.
au point que
extreme consequence
Il était malade, au point que le médecin a voulu l’hospitaliser.
d’où + noun
short conclusion
La terre est sèche, d’où l’importance d’arroser.
“D’où” is followed by a NOUN, not a verb: “d’où l’importance”, “d’où mon retard”, “d’où son succès”.
2. Intensity: si / tellement… que, tant de… que
To show that a cause is so strong that it produces a consequence:
si / tellement + adjective / adverb + que
Il a fait si chaud que les arbustes sont morts.
verb + tellement / tant + que
Il a tellement plu que les rues étaient inondées.
tant de / tellement de + noun + que
Il y avait tant de monde qu’on ne pouvait plus entrer.
un tel / une telle + noun + que
Il y avait une telle chaleur que les écoles ont fermé.
“Si” and “tellement” go before the adjective; “tant” CANNOT go before an adjective: “tant chaud” ✗ → “si chaud” or “tellement chaud”.
3. Purpose: pour que / afin que + subjunctive, pour / afin de + infinitive
Purpose is an intention, not an accomplished fact: that’s why it requires the SUBJUNCTIVE. If the subject is the same, you use the infinitive:
Different subjects → que + subjunctive
Same subject → de + infinitive
On arrose pour que la terre colle aux racines.
On arrose pour aider l’arbre.
Je fais un calendrier afin que les enfants s’en occupent.
Je fais un calendrier afin de les responsabiliser.
Elle parle fort pour qu’on l’entende.
Elle parle fort pour être entendue.
“Afin que / afin de” are more formal than “pour que / pour”. Other expressions of purpose: “dans le but de” + infinitive, “en vue de” + noun.
4. Negative purpose: de peur que, de crainte que
To avoid an outcome you fear. After “de peur que” an EXPLETIVE “ne” often appears, which is NOT a negation:
We put in a stake for fear the wind might flatten the tree. (the wind is NOT negated)
Not too close, for fear the roots might damage the wall.
She prepared the party in secret, for fear Nathalie would forbid it.
He stayed at home for fear of falling ill. (same subject → de + infinitive)
The expletive “ne” is optional and appears mostly in writing. “De peur que le vent couche l’arbre” is also correct. NEVER add “pas”: the meaning would be reversed!
5. “De sorte que”: consequence or purpose?
“De sorte que”, “de manière que” and “de façon que” have two meanings, depending on the mood of the verb:
real consequence
Il a creusé large, de sorte que les racines ont de la place.
intended purpose
Creusez large, de sorte que les racines aient de la place.
Tip: if you can replace it with “si bien que”, it’s a consequence (indicative). If you can replace it with “pour que”, it’s a purpose (subjunctive).
“We water so that the soil sticks to the roots.”
On arrose pour que la terre colle pas aux racines.
On arrose pour la terre colle aux racines.
“It was so hot that the shrubs died.”
Il faisait si chaud que les arbustes sont morts.
Il faisait tant chaud que les arbustes sont morts.
Il faisait si chaud pour que les arbustes sont morts.
In “de peur que le vent ne couche l’arbre”, “ne” is…
expletive (it doesn’t negate)

In September 2033, Rose-Hélène moved up to the top section, still at the school on rue Dumenge. It was her last year of nursery school. The following year she would go to the big school, where you learn to read. She was already talking about it with a mixture of impatience and suspicion. She had asked Julien whether you were allowed to bring a harmonica to the big school. Julien had said it would have to be negotiated.

Mrs Chevalier was still her teacher. She had asked to keep her for a third year, which was quite exceptional. The head had agreed, so Rose-Hélène would spend her whole nursery schooling with the same teacher, in the same classroom, with the same coat peg bearing her name. She found that normal. She said Mrs Chevalier needed her for the silence.

The “A tree for every school” programme announced by the minister during the summer had been launched at the start of the school year. Every school in France could ask for a free tree, planted in its playground before winter. The school on rue Dumenge was among the first to sign up. Mrs Chevalier had filled in the form on the first day of term, at seven in the morning, before the children had even arrived.

But which tree to choose? Mrs Chevalier asked the advice of Dr Lefèvre, the city botanist, whom all of La Duchère had known since the summer. Dr Lefèvre came one Tuesday afternoon in her straw hat and gave a lesson to the top-section children, sitting in a circle on the ground in the playground. Rose-Hélène was in the front row. She had brought a notebook, like Amina.

Dr Lefèvre explained that summers were going to get hotter and hotter, so trees able to withstand drought had to be chosen. She showed photos. A plane tree, too big for the playground. A holm oak, too slow to grow. And a silver lime, a cousin of the La Duchère lime tree, whose leaves had a white underside that reflected the sunlight, so that the tree stayed cooler.

The children voted. Twenty-two votes for the silver lime, one for the plane tree, and one for “a sweet tree”, proposed by a little boy called Lucas. Dr Lefèvre promised to plant the silver lime in November, when the soil would be damp enough for the roots to settle before the cold. She added that, for the sweet tree, they would have to wait for a few more years of research.

Meanwhile, in Bucharest, work on the Stan house was beginning. On Monday 12 September, Ioana and Sorina took the six a.m. flight to be there for the first day on site. Andrei had come from London. Mr Ciobanu had brought in a team of fifteen workers, two Arhimar architects and an enormous crane truck, parked in front of the house, which blocked the whole street.

The crane truck had a very specific mission. Before work began, the piano had to be taken out of the house so that it wouldn’t be damaged by dust and vibrations. But the grand piano was too big to go down the stairs. It had come into the house in 1907 through the big balcony window, before the balcony had even been built. So it would leave by the same route, a hundred and twenty-six years later.

Viorica was there, of course. She had been sitting on her bench opposite since seven in the morning, in her black coat and veiled hat, despite the September heat. She had been ninety-three since August. She had refused to stay at home, for fear the piano would be damaged in her absence. She wanted to watch every move the workers made. Nobody dared contradict her.

The operation took three hours. The workers first dismantled the wave balcony, piece by piece, numbering every bit of wrought iron so it could be put back exactly as before. Then they removed the big window. Then they wrapped the piano in thick blankets, tied it with straps and hooked it to the crane’s arm. The whole street held its breath.

At a quarter past eleven, the piano came out of the first-floor window. It swung slowly in mid-air above the pavement, black and huge in its blankets, like a sleeping animal. Passers-by had stopped. The neighbours were at their windows. And on her bench, Viorica had both hands clenched on her cane, so tightly that her knuckles were white. She had stopped breathing.

The piano came down centimetre by centimetre, onto the truck of the restorer, Mr Petrescu, who was waiting below with his arms outstretched, like a father receiving a child. When the piano touched the floor of the truck, the whole street applauded. Viorica closed her eyes. Then she said to Ioana, sitting next to her: “It left the way it came in. That’s a good sign. It means it will come back.”

Mr Petrescu took the piano to his workshop on the other side of the city, a former stable turned into a restoration room, where three hundred-year-old pianos were already waiting their turn. He began by taking it apart completely, piece by piece, so that he could examine every component. He numbered the eighty-eight hammers, the two hundred and thirty strings, the hundreds of small pieces of wood and felt. He said a piano was a whole city.

On the third day, removing the keyboard, he found something. Slipped under the keys, right at the back, against the wooden case, was a yellowed envelope. It was sealed. On the envelope, in fine, slanting handwriting, it said in French: “For whoever opens this piano. March 1950.” Mr Petrescu didn’t open the envelope. He put it in a box and called Ioana, who was still in Bucharest.

They took the envelope to Viorica that same evening. The old lady recognised the handwriting at once. It was her father’s. She opened the envelope with a butter knife, her hands trembling. Inside was a single sheet, folded in four. She read it in silence. Then she handed it to Ioana. Viorica’s father had written three lines, the day before the confiscation, knowing he would probably never see his piano again.

“Whoever you are, I entrust this instrument to you. Tune it, so that it sings again. And if one day a child plays it, tell them that an old man locked it so that it would not be sad while waiting for them.” Viorica held the letter to her chest throughout dinner. She hardly ate anything. At the end she said her father had waited eighty-three years for an answer. Now he had been answered.

Ioana stayed in Bucharest for a week to get the site going. She worked with the Arhimar architects, organised the teams, checked the plans. She spoke Romanian on site and French on the phone with Lyon, so that by the end of the week she was dreaming in both languages at once. Sorina was going to stay in Bucharest for three months to follow the work day to day.

In the evenings, Ioana often had dinner at Viorica’s, in her little ground-floor flat next to the site. The old lady cooked dishes from her childhood, recipes she hadn’t made for years for lack of guests. She talked. Ioana listened. One evening, Viorica asked her whether she knew why she had been so set on saving the house. Ioana said she thought she knew. Viorica shook her head.

“It isn’t for my father,” she said. “Or for the piano. It’s so that one day someone will open this door without knowing it was closed for sixty years. A child who will come in here to learn the violin and who will know nothing of all that. That’s what I want. For the misfortune to be forgotten, so that only the music remains.” She poured Ioana more tea. Then she changed the subject.

Sorina had moved in with her mother, in a small flat in the Cotroceni district, twenty minutes from the site. She left every morning at seven and rarely came home before nine at night. Andrei came from London once a month, as promised, then twice a month, without anyone asking him. He said it was to follow the work more closely. Sorina asked no questions. Viorica, on her bench, smiled.

In October, Grandma came from Iași by train with Elena to see the site. She spent the afternoon on the bench with Viorica, watching the workers climb up and down the scaffolding. The two old ladies commented on everything, like two foremen. They noticed that one of the workers wasn’t wearing his helmet, and they pointed it out so firmly that he never took it off again, not even to eat.

In Lyon, meanwhile, something important had happened that nobody had foreseen. One Thursday in October, after the adult orchestra’s rehearsal, Mr Vidal didn’t look at his watch. He didn’t mention his 21:34 train. He had his coffee with Amina at the station buffet as usual, and instead of heading for the platform he stayed at the counter. Amina asked him whether he was going to miss his train.

He replied that he had no train any more. He had applied in the spring for a transfer to the regional audit chamber in Lyon, and it had just been accepted. He would start on 1 November. He had already found a flat in Croix-Rousse, a ten-minute walk from the Salle Hélène Morel. He had chosen it so that it would be near the hall. He didn’t say so, but Amina understood.

Amina said nothing for a long moment. She stirred her coffee with her spoon, even though she never took sugar. Then she took out her phone, opened the Thursday orchestra spreadsheet, and deleted the column headed “B. V. train times”. She did it slowly, very carefully. Then she put her phone away and said simply: “Welcome to Lyon.”

The move took place on Saturday 29 October. Mr Vidal had hardly anything: a few boxes of books, grey suits, a bed, a table and his violin. Amina came to help, with a spreadsheet of the boxes, of course. Isabelle gave him an old lamp of Odile’s, so that the flat would be less bare. And Bernard Delorme, who had a van, moved everything in a single trip, singing brass-band tunes out of tune.

It was the first time she had used “tu” with him. Mr Vidal noticed. He said nothing either. But the following Thursday at rehearsal, when Théo asked everyone to play a note of their choice to tune up, he played a very soft, very long A, looking at Amina’s triangle. And Amina, for the first time, struck her triangle outside the silence. Just once. To answer.

Théo saw the look. So did Isabelle. Bernard Delorme, who never noticed anything, asked out loud why everyone was smiling. The baker elbowed him so hard he nearly dropped his trumpet. Nobody explained anything. But in “The Thursday Ducks” group that evening there were three hundred and twelve messages. Amina, who was in the group, didn’t read a single one.

On Monday 1 November, Mr Vidal started at the regional audit chamber, in a big stone building on the banks of the Rhône. His new colleagues had heard about him: the magistrate who had audited the “Musique en partage” network and come back with a violin. On the first day, someone had put a music stand on his desk. He never removed it.

In Corsica, meanwhile, the plans for the new school had been presented to the village. Hugo had drawn them throughout September with a passion Ioana had never seen in him. He had put the music room in the centre, between the two classrooms, with a large picture window onto the square, so that from the room you would see the lime tree. Antoine had looked at the plans for a long time. Then he had asked where the bench would be.

Hugo hadn’t drawn a bench. He added a stone bench in front of the picture window, facing the tree, in the next version of the plans. He called it “Antoine’s bench”. Antoine said it was ridiculous, that you don’t name a bench after yourself while you’re alive. Then he asked whether the bench would be in the shade. Hugo said that depended on the tree. If it came back to life, yes. Antoine nodded. He said it would be in the shade.

Antoine was getting weaker. He had had pneumonia in October, to the point that the doctor had wanted to admit him to hospital in Bastia. He had refused. He said he had a tree to water and a little girl to wait for in the spring. He still watered, but less. He no longer carried the bucket. The three women did, taking turns. He poured the water. He said it was the gesture that counted, not the weight.

Rose-Hélène sent Antoine a drawing every week by post, with her father’s help for the address. She always drew the same thing: a tree with green leaves, lots of green leaves, and an old man beside it with a bucket. The music teacher told Julien that Antoine hung the drawings on the wall of the wash house with clothes pegs. By the end of November there were twelve. People from the village came to look at them.

On Tuesday 15 November, Dr Lefèvre planted the silver lime in the playground of the school on rue Dumenge. It was cold and grey. The twenty-four top-section children stood in a circle around the hole, in hats and scarves. Each had brought a handful of earth from home, so that the tree would have a little of every house. Rose-Hélène had brought a handful of earth from the foot of the La Duchère lime tree.

Dr Lefèvre explained every step so that the children would understand. You had to dig wide so that the roots had room. You had to water straight away, even in November, so that the soil would stick to the roots. You had to put in a stake, for fear the wind would flatten the young tree. And you needed patience. A lot of patience. A lime tree, she said, takes twenty years to become a real tree.

During the planting, a few snowflakes fell, the first of the winter. The children looked up, shouting. Dr Lefèvre said it was perfect: the snow would melt slowly, so that the water would seep gently down to the roots. Rose-Hélène emptied her handful of La Duchère earth into the bottom of the hole, last, just before the tree was put in. She didn’t tell anyone where that earth came from.

Twenty years. The children did the sum with Mrs Chevalier. In twenty years they would be twenty-five. Lucas, the sweet-tree boy, declared he would be too old to enjoy the shade. Mrs Chevalier replied that that was exactly the point: you plant trees so that other children can enjoy them. Lucas thought about it. Then he said that in that case, he wanted his name written somewhere.

So Mrs Chevalier had an idea. She had a small wooden plaque made, fixed to the stake, with the class’s twenty-four first names and a sentence the children chose together after a very close vote: “We planted it for you. Water it for those who come next.” Rose-Hélène had suggested adding “and whistle three notes to it”, but the proposal got only two votes.

The two votes were hers and Lucas’s, who had voted for her in exchange for a promise: that she would teach him to whistle. She kept her promise. All through December, at every break, you could see two five-year-olds sitting at the foot of the young silver lime, one blowing with all his might without producing the slightest sound, the other explaining very seriously where to put his tongue.

At the beginning of December it was so cold that Mrs Chevalier feared for the young lime tree. One morning, arriving at school, she found the little trunk wrapped in six scarves of different colours, tied on by the children the evening before, at the end of the day, without her noticing. Dr Lefèvre, called in urgently, said the tree didn’t need scarves. Then she said they could be left. They wouldn’t do it any harm.

On Wednesday 14 December, the Thursday orchestra gave a special concert, on a Wednesday, in the geriatric ward of the Croix-Rousse hospital, where Nadia had worked nights for twenty years. It was her idea. The fourteen musicians set up in the corridor, between the rooms, so that the patients could hear from their beds. They played the march, the Romanian tune and the waltz. The nurses cried.

In the last room along the corridor was the old patient whom Nadia had sent to sleep in the spring with a single flute note. She was ninety-four. She no longer spoke much. But at the moment of silence in the waltz, when Amina struck her triangle, she raised her hand, very slowly, and made a gesture towards Nadia. The gesture of a conductor giving the cue. Nadia played her G.

December was also the month of Nathalie’s departure. She had set her last day at the firm for Friday 16 December. She didn’t want a party. She had said so again and again to everyone: Ioana, Sophie, Hugo, Karim, the interns. No speeches, no presents, no champagne. She wanted to leave the way she had arrived in 1998: discreetly, with a single cardboard box.

Of course, nobody listened to her. For three weeks, the team secretly prepared a party, for fear Nathalie would find out and forbid it. Sophie had done the budget. Karim was in charge of the music. Hugo had found in the archives the plans of Nathalie’s first project, a little house in Villeurbanne drawn in 1998 on her second-hand table. And Ioana had called Mr Ciobanu in Bucharest.

Ioana, for her part, was afraid. In two weeks she would be alone at the head of the firm. She slept badly. She redid the accounts at night, reread contracts, imagined every possible disaster. One evening, Julien found her in the kitchen at two in the morning, in front of a forecast spreadsheet. He took her hand. He reminded her of what Nathalie had told her a year earlier: “You learn by doing it.” Ioana closed the computer. She went to bed.

On Friday 16 December at five p.m., Nathalie packed her last things into her cardboard box. Her pencils, her spare glasses, a photo of herself at thirty on a building site, and the old wooden ruler she had always used. She switched off her computer. She looked at her empty desk. Then she picked up her box, opened her office door, and stopped dead.

In the big open-plan office, all the lights were off except one. In the middle of the room, on a table, under a single lamp, was a model. It was the little house in Villeurbanne, her first project, rebuilt in cardboard by Hugo and the interns, to the millimetre, from the 1998 plans. Around the table, in the half-light, the firm’s fourteen employees were waiting in silence.

Nathalie put her box down on the floor. She went up to the model. She recognised every detail: the little round bathroom window, the outside staircase, the mistake she had made on the slope of the roof and had had to correct on site. Hugo had reproduced the mistake, then the correction, with a little piece of cardboard of a different colour. Nathalie laughed. Then she began to cry.

Then the lights came back on and the party began, despite all her protests. There was champagne, contrary to her orders. There were speeches, contrary to her orders. Sophie read a poem she had written, very bad and very moving. Karim played the guitar. And on a big screen at the back of the room appeared the face of Mr Ciobanu, live from Bucharest.

He wasn’t alone. Beside him, in front of the Stan house under renovation, under a site floodlight, were Sorina, Andrei, the whole team of workers in yellow helmets and, sitting on her bench in her black coat, Viorica. They were holding a handwritten banner in French, with spelling mistakes: “Thank you Nathalie for the bridge”. Nathalie looked at the screen without understanding. Then she understood.

Because, deep down, she was the one who had made it all possible. If she hadn’t founded the firm in 1998, if she hadn’t hired a young Romanian architect who spoke poor French, if she hadn’t offered that young architect a partnership, then the firm, there would never have been a bridge between Lyon and Bucharest. Viorica raised her hand towards the screen. Nathalie raised hers.

At the end of the evening, Nathalie took Ioana aside, by the window overlooking rue de la République lit up for Christmas. She asked whether she had kept the old rusty key. Ioana took it out of her pocket. She had carried it with her for a year. Nathalie smiled. She said she had one last thing to entrust to her, to keep with the key.

It was the old wooden ruler, the one she had put in her cardboard box. It was worn, ink-stained, and one edge was slightly warped. “It isn’t very straight any more,” said Nathalie. “I used it for thirty-five years, so it has taken the shape of my hand. It will take time to take the shape of yours. But it will get there. Like the firm.”

That evening, back on rue d’Austerlitz, Ioana put the ruler and the key side by side on the kitchen table. Julien looked at them for a long time. He said they looked like a coat of arms. Rose-Hélène, who wasn’t asleep, came to look. She picked up the ruler, measured it with her hand, then asked what it was for. Ioana answered: for drawing straight lines. Rose-Hélène pointed out that it was crooked.

Ioana laughed. She said that was true, and that was exactly why it was precious. Perfectly straight lines could be drawn with any ruler. This one drew lines that had lived. Rose-Hélène thought about it. Then she said it was like the silence in the waltz: it wasn’t perfect either, since everyone whistled out of tune. But it was the most beautiful moment.

On 23 December, for what would have been Odile’s eighty-third birthday, the family gathered at Isabelle’s, as every year. But this year there were two more guests. Nathalie, who had come with her box of chocolates and without her ruler. And Mr Vidal, whom Amina had brought without telling anyone, saying simply that he now lived ten minutes away. Isabelle added two chairs.

During dinner, Grandma video-called from Iași, as every 23 December. She said she had seen Viorica’s piano in Mr Petrescu’s workshop, in pieces, and that it had had the same effect on her as a pig being cut up for Christmas. The whole table laughed. Then Yves Le Goff, who had turned ninety the day before and was spending Christmas in Nantes, sent a photo of his cake. There was a single candle, shaped like a boat.

After dinner, Mr Vidal took out his Mirecourt violin. Isabelle took her cello. Amina put her triangle on the table, next to the coffee cups. And they played Henri’s waltz, as a trio, in Odile’s living room, in front of the empty armchair and the blue shawl. It was the first time the Thursday orchestra had played in someone’s home. It was a small orchestra. Three musicians, two of them beginners.

At the third verse, they stopped. Eight bars. In the middle of the silence, Amina struck her triangle. Ting. Then Rose-Hélène played the three notes on the harmonica. Henri-Ion, who was almost three, whistled a real note for the first time, just one, very faint, but in tune. Little Yves, on Lucia’s knees, clapped his hands. And Nathalie, who didn’t know the waltz, whistled the rest along with everyone.

Later, when everyone had gone, Rose-Hélène asked her father whether trees could be planted in winter. Julien said yes, in November or December, when the ground was damp. She asked whether trees planted in winter grew in the spring. Julien said yes, if they were watered. She nodded. She was thinking of a black tree in a square in Corsica, and an old shepherd who was waiting for her.

Before falling asleep, she opened the box of Henri’s harmonica, where she kept Antoine’s letter. She couldn’t read yet, but she knew the letter by heart. She recited it softly in the dark, to be sure not to forget it: “If I’m no longer here in spring, come and see if it has leaves.” Then she closed the box and whistled three notes, very softly, towards the window. For Corsica.

Reading: The planting guide

The sheet Dr Lefèvre wrote for all the Lyon schools taking part in the “A tree for every school” programme. Notice how each piece of advice comes with its purpose or consequence. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Planter un arbre à l’école : mode d’emploi
Choose a tree suited to tomorrow’s climate. Summers will get hotter and hotter, so fragile species will not survive. Prefer the silver lime, the nettle tree or the holm oak.
Plant between November and February, so that the roots have time to settle before the heat. A tree planted in spring suffers so much in its first summer that it often dies.
Dig a hole twice as wide as the root ball, so that the roots can spread easily. Don’t place it too close to buildings, for fear the roots might damage the foundations.
Put in a stake so that the wind doesn’t flatten the young tree. Water generously on planting day, even in winter, in order to firm the soil well around the roots.
The first year is decisive, hence the importance of a watering calendar. Entrust it to the children: they will be so proud of their tree that they will never forget it.
Finally, be patient. A tree takes twenty years to give real shade. You will not plant it for yourselves, but so that your pupils’ children can one day play at its foot. — Dr Claire Lefèvre
